title: Bereshit: why begin with bet?
hookLine: the Torah opens with its second letter, closed on three sides and open ahead (Genesis Rabbah 1:10)

lines: A TINY THING IS A DOOR.
cards: Every alphabet starts somewhere. English starts with A. Hebrew starts with aleph.
So you'd expect the Torah to start with aleph. It doesn't. Its very first word is Bereshit, in the beginning, and it starts with the second letter, bet.
The rabbis noticed, and asked: why would the Torah skip its own first letter? It seems like a tiny thing. But in the study hall, a tiny thing is a door.

teach.b: The first verse, in English: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." In Hebrew, the first word is Bereshit, and its first letter is bet. Look at its shape.

It's like a square bracket: a line along the top, a line down the right side, a line along the bottom, and open on the left. Hebrew reads right to left, so that open side faces forward, into the rest of the text.
The midrash, Genesis Rabbah, asks: why was the world created with a bet?

teach.h: CLOSED ON THREE SIDES, OPEN AHEAD.
teach.b: Because just as the bet is closed on three sides and open on one, you are not meant to ask what is above, what is below, what came before. Only from the day the world was created, and onward. It's a surprising answer.
It sets a limit: some questions, about what came before the beginning, are closed. But it opens a road: everything after is yours to explore. The same passage gives another reason.
Bet begins bracha, blessing; aleph begins a word for curse. So the Torah starts with the letter of blessing. And Rashi, whom you met last week, adds a grammar puzzle.
The first words, he says, don't quite mean in the beginning.
They mean something closer to, in the beginning of God's creating. Read that way, the verse isn't listing what was made first; it's the start of a longer sentence.
So the Torah opens mid-sentence, with a letter that looks forward.
The midrash puts the lesson in its shape: a wall behind, and the way open ahead.

how: Parashat Bereshit, Genesis 1:1–6:8, is read on the Shabbat after Simchat Torah, and students traditionally begin their study of it with Rashi's comments on the first verse.

games.q: you're a student in the study hall. you notice the Torah starts with bet, not aleph. what do you do?
o: ignore it; a letter is just a letter.
games.why: the rabbis asked. their answer: bet is closed on three sides and open ahead, and it's the letter of blessing.

practice: Picture the letter bet: a roof, a wall behind you, a floor, and an open side in front. Let the wall be everything already done, yesterday's mistakes, old worries, what you can't change, holding you up instead of pulling you back.
Then look toward the open side, and find one step ahead of you today, just one.
